data.title: VerilyMe, Bausch + Lomb partner up on dry eye education
data.description:
Personalized AI health app VerilyMe is visualizing expanded eye health education in a new partnership with eye health-focused drugmaker Bausch + Lomb. 

The companies are joining forces in an initial collaboration focused on dry eye disease, a common but underdiagnosed condition that impacts some 150 million U.S. adults. Through VerilyMe’s digital platform, the partners offer expanded information about dry eye disease risk factors, symptoms and treatment options with new content that launched on the app in June. 

Bausch + Lomb chose Verily as its partner on the digital front to continue its mission of helping patients better understand eye health, seeing evolving technology and AI capabilities as “critical” for patients in making health choices, Bausch + Lomb’s SVP and general manager, North America Pharmaceuticals Yolande Barnard explained in an interview with Fierce Pharma Marketing. 

VerilyMe, meanwhile, is a free digital wellness app rooted in preventative healthcare strategies. The app launched last October and emerged from beta mode in February, and works by offering access to speedy, accurate health insights by connecting users to licensed clinicians who can provide secure health recommendations based on their medical records. 

On Verily’s side, “we couldn’t think of a better partner” from the pharmaceutical industry to help drive forward eye care information that can “guide people to have a better life,” Verily’s chief physician executive Vindell Washington, M.D. added. 

Related

Verily Health simplifies medical jargon alphabet soup with AI-powered app in new campaign

Although dry eye disease is prevalent, it’s a “very complex” disease with a significant “need for information,” Barnard said, pointing to a dry eye disease survey that found that 78% of patients desire greater educational resources. 

Dry eye disease is just the starting point for the collaboration between VerilyMe and Bausch + Lomb. Vision problems is one in which patients “really suffer” without appropriate care, Barnard explained. However, eye conditions can often be brushed off as a natural offshoot of aging or as something that may not require as much immediate attention. 

“Think about the impact of patients’ quality of life when we are suffering through eye conditions,” Barnard said. “This is certainly something that motivates us to make a difference.”

To her point, Bausch + Lomb’s latest State of Dry Eye survey found that one in five dry eye sufferers reported that the symptoms impact their confidence (22%) and emotional wellbeing (20%), as well as increasing stress and anxiety levels. However, 59% marked improved emotional wellbeing upon using a prescription treatment.  

With VerilyMe, Bausch + Lomb can not only help improve eye health but quality of life for patients who may be suffering from vision concerns and eye diseases. 

“It closes these gaps. It helps a patient easily navigate ‘hey, what is going on with me? What could this be?’” Barnard said of the VerilyMe collaboration. 

Verily has embarked on similar collaborations in the past surrounding medical devices and other specific disease types, but its work with Bausch + Lomb is unique in that it can help provide more personalized information and focus specifically on distributing information to a curated group of people “most in need” of specific health information, Washington said. 

For Bausch + Lomb, meanwhile, the partnership is the company’s first large collab on a digital platform. 

“There is a huge amount of information out there, but for a patient to truly understand what is accurate, what is specific – this is where it becomes quite challenging,” Barnard explained. “So this is a one stop shop where they know that this is accurate, personalized information.”

At the intersection of health and AI, Verily keeps patient safety top of mind, including a “series of guardrails” and being mindful of keeping up standards that wouldn’t present “unsafe environments.” 

“Although we plan to advance our AI more and more in the future, we’re going to advance it under this umbrella of respect for patients, patient safety and efficacy,” Washington said. 

Barnard and Bausch + Lomb agree: “there is no compromise” around patient safety, she emphasized. 

For Verily, the partnership solidifies a new chapter for the company after splitting off from Alphabet in March, transitioning to its own corporation more than ten years after its 2015 inception as a moonshot of Google X. Meanwhile, Bausch + Lomb is embarking on the new technology-driven path as an expansion of its dry eye expertise, with leading eye drop Miebo and its other dry eye products picking up a total haul of $1.1 billion last year.

data.title: FDA approves Takeda's first-in-class Orzeyful for narcolepsy
data.description:
After coming up short in trials with two orexin type 2 receptor (OX2R) selective agonists, Takeda has scored with oveporexton, gaining FDA approval for the first-in-clas,s twice-daily tablet as a treatment for adults with narcolepsy type 1 (NT1).

Rather than addressing the symptoms of narcolepsy, Orzeyful—as it will be known commercially—becomes the first medicine to address its root cause, doing so by mimicking the body’s orexin cycle. Orexin is a neuropeptide lacking in patients with narcolepsy that helps regulate waking, wakefulness, appetite and energy. 

“The FDA approval of Orzeyful marks a new chapter for the narcolepsy type 1 community, as we introduce an entirely new class of medicine that will potentially redefine how this disease is managed and how people feel on treatment,” Takeda CEO Julie Kim said in a statement.

Takeda has a lot riding on Orzeyful, pegging its peak sales at between $2 billion and $3 billion. It is one of three potential blockbusters the Japanese company is counting on as it faces biosimilar competition for its top-selling product Entyvio.

NT1 is a neurological condition driven by the loss of orexin, affecting roughly 120,000 people in the U.S., many of whom remain undiagnosed. NT1 causes daytime sleepiness, cataplexy (sudden loss of muscle tone), cognitive symptoms, disrupted nighttime sleep and hallucinations.

Julie Flygare, who is the CEO at Project Sleep and an NT1 patient, called the approval “a historic moment,” as it “expands our treatment choices.”

The approval is backed by two phase 3 studies which showed that Orzeyful, compared to placebo, provides statistically significant improvements in daytime sleepiness, cataplexy and health-related quality of life measures. 

No serious treatment-related adverse events were reported in the trials. The most common side effects were insomnia and urinary urgency and frequency.

Takeda will launch Orzeyful after the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) completes its controlled substance classification review, which is expected within the next 90 days. The company added that it does not expect Orzeyful sales to significantly impact its revenue forecast for the fiscal year, which ends on March 31, 2027.

The success of Orzeyful comes after the company’s first attempt in the indication with an OX2R agonist, TAK-994, was halted five years ago in two phase 2 trials because of liver toxicity issues. Then, two years ago, Takeda grounded OX2R agonist danavorexton (TAK-925) because of slow enrollment in a phase 2 trial testing the intravenous treatment in post-surgical patients with obstructive sleep apnea.

Related

Takeda looks toward 'inflection point' as it eyes new launches to shake off Vyvanse generic impacts

Takeda hopes to gain FDA approval for another first-in-class treatment later in this quarter as rusfertide is under review for the blood disorder polycythemia vera. The injected hepcidin mimetic peptide, which was acquired in a $300 million licensing deal with Protagonist Therapeutics in 2024, scored in a phase 3 trial last year. Takeda expects that rusfertide has the potential to bring between $1 billion and $2 billion in peak sales.

Takeda’s highest hopes in its pipeline are for Entyvio follow-on zasocitinib. The TYK2 inhibitor, which was secured in a $4 billion upfront deal with Nimbus Therapeutics four years ago, has the potential to become the top oral drug in the in psoriasis and psoriatic arthritis, according to Takeda, drawing a peak sales forecast of between $3 billion and $6 billion. Last month, the company unveiled additional data from a successful phase 3 study of zasocitinib.

data.title: ViiV targets ‘future you’ in long-acting HIV campaign
data.description:
HIV drugmaker ViiV Healthcare is helping prospective HIV prevention or treatment users to make a choice that will help them later down the line in its “Do It For Future You” campaign. 

The multichannel campaign positions ViiV’s collection of long-acting injectable options for HIV treatment and prevention as a way for people to take greater control of their health and future and looks to spark more discussions with healthcare providers about long-acting options, the company explained in an Aug. 4 press release. 

“Do It For Future You” is ViiV’s umbrella campaign that centers on the idea that “the choices you make today shape your tomorrow,” the company’s head of enterprise communications, Bithiah Lafontant, explained in an interview with Fierce Pharma Marketing. 

“Sometimes it's easy to get caught up in the day-to-day of life, and you're not really being proactive about the health choices that you're making,” Lafontant said. “We want people to stop for a minute and think about how the choices they make today are impactful in the future.”

The campaign roll-out features a dedicated website that hosts resources and information on treatment and prevention options as well as a video that brings the message to life. 

The video sees three interconnected scenes of young adults, with dialogue and laughter interspersed with soft background music and a voiceover telling viewers to “do it for the you who’s still becoming.”

“The future doesn’t begin someday,” the voiceover says later in the video. “It begins right now, with what you do next. With a conversation. A question. A choice you can feel good about.” 

In one scene, a young couple at a party runs off, ending up in a lit-up gazebo and sharing a moment before more friends join. Another sees a group of friends driving with the top down at night in a car lit up with blue neon lights, filming each other as they wave bubble blasters and dance before later stopping at a food truck. 

Also woven into the video is a young woman training in the boxing ring, who falls again and again at one point before getting back up and locking in. The ad continues to cut between scenes, showing moments like the couple running through a sprinkler, the athlete nailing her targets and the friend group dancing and doing model struts down the sidewalk.  

“Talk to your doctor about long-acting injectable HIV prevention and treatment options,” the voiceover continues, advising viewers to “make a choice that fits your life.”

By the end of the video, the boxer embraces her trainer and pumps her fists in celebration, while the couple kisses and the video pivots back to the laughing friends in the back of the car as the “do it for future you” tagline appears on-screen.  

“Don’t wait. The future isn’t far off. It’s already here,” the voiceover says at the end. 

The nostalgic, flashbulb-memory feel that the video has is on purpose, Lafontant said, as it aims to capture the small moments that one might not consider important until later in life. One of those moments may be the decision to talk to a provider about HIV options. 

Related

ViiV launches ‘Still Here’ campaign aimed at reminding young people about HIV

“We want people to be able to live healthy lives and have fun with their family and their friends and their loved ones, and so we think that by focusing on people's sexual health and making sure that they're empowered to talk to their providers, we're moving in that direction,” she added. 

To continue to spread the word, the company will extend its digital strategy to out-of-home marketing later this summer in specific priority markets including Atlanta and Los Angeles, according to Lafontant. So far, ViiV has gotten a “great response” and hopes to continue the campaign for “a time to come.” 

ViiV strived to ensure that “anybody can see themselves” in the concepts presented, Lafontant said, and therefore included a diverse cast for the video across genders, races and sexuality. Diversity in HIV also extends to treatment options—Lafontant emphasized that there are “options that can fit anybody’s life,” as some may prefer an oral treatment or preventative to a long-acting injectable. 

“We know there are people for whom a daily pill is going to be something that’s perfect for their lives,” but for other people, “that just doesn’t fit,” Lafontant explained. 

ViiV’s own pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) injectable Apretude first hit the U.S. market in 2021 as the world’s first long-acting PrEP option, touting an every-two-month dosing schedule. Earlier that year, the company had taken its long-acting HIV treatment Cabenuva across the FDA finish line, with its once-monthly dosing later expanded to every two months as well.  

Still, despite the evolution of the HIV market into the long-acting space, the HIV epidemic is still raging on with more than 39,000 diagnoses in the U.S. annually, according to ViiV. As it stands, only some 25% of people who could benefit from PrEP are currently receiving it, while nearly one third of people living with HIV in the U.S. have not achieved viral suppression.

As long-acting injectable options are a more recent development in the HIV landscape, the new options may be key to ending the HIV epidemic for good. So far, with daily oral options the norm for years, “the needle isn’t moving,” Lafontant said. 

“We’re really hopeful that as long-acting options become more familiar, more people will select to go down that road and we’ll finally start to see those numbers moving in the direction.” 

While ViiV was the first to open the long-acting door, Gilead Sciences has more recently entered the space with its twice-yearly Yeztugo. Next up on the horizon is Merck and its alimatravir, a once-monthly oral PrEP option that’s currently being studied in phase 3 trials.

data.title: Moderna's mRNA flu shot nabs FDA nod after earlier review hiccup
data.description:
Despite a major curveball thrown by the FDA earlier this year, Moderna has managed to strike true with a U.S. approval for its mRNA-based influenza vaccine. 

The FDA on late Wednesday signed off on Moderna’s vaccine, christened mFlusiva, to prevent seasonal influenza in all adults ages 50 years and older. With the green light, Moderna has scooped up its fourth FDA nod and cleared the way for the first-ever flu shot leveraging mRNA technology in the United States. 

The vaccine’s odds of approval stateside were thrown into flux in February when the FDA issued Moderna a rare refusal to file (RTF) letter, citing concerns with the design of the phase 3 trial for the shot, at the time known as mRNA-1010. 

Moderna publicly pushed back against the FDA’s decision not to take up its application, and the agency—whose Center for Biologics Evaluation and Research (CBER) responsible for vaccines was at the time headed up by controversial director Vinay Prasad, M.D.—reversed course a little over a week later.

Related

With the FDA's Moderna decision, vaccine makers face increasingly uncertain regulatory environment

The FDA’s concerns specifically came down to the use of a standard-dose flu vaccine as the comparator arm in one of the trial’s supporting mFlusiva’s approval. The FDA at the time suggested that it had issues because Moderna had not used “the best-available standard of care” in its study—a position the company disagreed with and noted that the FDA had not flagged as a problem when previously discussing trial protocols. 

At one additional checkpoint on the way to approval, the FDA’s Vaccines and Related Biological Products Advisory Committee voted unanimously that mFlusiva’s benefits outweighed its risks across both the 50-to-64-year age group and in patients ages 65 years and older.

With regards to those age groups, mFlusiva has secured a traditional FDA approval in the 50-to-64-year bracket and an accelerated nod in the older group. The decision was backed up by data from a pair of phase 3 trials, with the study in the younger patient group comparing mFlusiva’s relative vaccine efficacy, among other measures, against a standard-dose comparator shot. The study in adults ages 65 and up pitted mFlusiva against a high-dose inactivated flu shot but with immunogenicity as the primary objective.

As required by an accelerated approval, Moderna noted that it will run a postmarketing trial to confirm its vaccine’s benefit in the older patient population. 

With the colder months drawing nearer, Moderna says it expects to make mFlusiva available in the U.S. for the 2026-2027 respiratory virus season. The new vaccine will join the stable of Moderna’s other mRNA vaccines Spikevax and mNexspike for COVID-19, and mResvia in respiratory syncytial virus. 

"The FDA approval of mFlusiva, our fourth approved product in the United States and the first mRNA-based flu vaccine, demonstrates the continued strength and versatility of our mRNA platform," Moderna helmsman Stéphane Bancel said in a Wednesday statement. 

"Flu remains a significant public health challenge, and mFlusiva provides an important new option for America's seniors,” he continued. “This approval also reflects the ongoing potential of our mRNA platform to help address important public health challenges through continued scientific innovation.”

Related

Moderna hires Novartis vet to lead commercial, upsizes role for Hoge as potential launches loom

Outside the U.S., Moderna’s mFlusiva application has been taken under review in the European Union, Canada and Australia. 

While the solo flu shot is awaiting a verdict in Europe, the EMA’s Committee for Medicinal Products for Human Use (CHMP) recommended approval for Moderna’s mCombriax in patients ages 50 and up. That mRNA vaccine is designed to confer protection against COVID and flu in a single combo shot.

data.title: Sanofi asked to change Dupixent ads after Galderma challenge
data.description:
Galderma Laboratories has landed a blow on Sanofi in its multi-case advertising row, driving the French drugmaker to change or drop certain claims about its blockbuster medicine Dupixent.

Last year, the BBB National Programs’ National Advertising Division (NAD) ruled against Galderma in two cases brought by Sanofi. In October, the NAD recommended that Galderma change or drop some claims about Nemluvio, an IL-31 drug that, like Dupixent, is used to treat prurigo nodularis (PN) and eczema. Two months later, the NAD recommended that Galderma change or drop other claims about Nemluvio.

Now, Galderma has struck back. Following a challenge by Galderma, the NAD recommended that Sanofi change or drop claims linking Dupixent to long-lasting clearer skin and fast itch relief. The U.S. advertising self-regulatory body also advised Sanofi to change or drop a prescriber-facing Day 2 itch relief claim. 

The NAD found that Sanofi’s evidence supports claims that some adults achieved clearer skin lasting four months to one year and that some experienced itch relief two weeks after the first dose. However, the advertising body recommended that Sanofi revise its TV claims to “clearly and conspicuously” disclose the response rate and that Dupixent was used in combination with topical corticosteroids.

An animated consumer-facing mechanism-of-action video likely conveyed the unsupported message that inhibition of IL-4 and IL-13 signaling alone is sufficient to address eczema, the NAD said. Dupixent targets IL-4 and IL-13.

Sanofi’s prescriber-facing claim that Dupixent reduced itch “starting as early as Day 2” was another cause of contention. The NAD found the post hoc analysis underpinning the claim failed to support Sanofi’s message that Dupixent demonstrated a meaningful treatment benefit beginning as early as Day 2. In its advertiser statement, Sanofi said that it “will comply with NAD’s recommendations.”

Galderma’s challenges to other Sanofi claims failed. The NAD found support for claims that Dupixent helps patients “stay ahead of eczema” and can “help heal your skin from within,” as well as for Sanofi’s statement that many adults saw 90% clearer skin. Sanofi can continue to make the 90% claim, although the NAD recommended against overstating the supporting evidence or obscuring the treatment context. 

The NAD sided with Sanofi on the question of whether its ads conveyed the message that Dupixent is superior to all other FDA-approved eczema treatments. Galderma also failed to persuade the NAD that the challenged ads implied Dupixent prevents eczema progression and blocks the most important source of inflammation.

Sanofi and Galderma are rowing over ads amid a fight for market share. Dupixent is a multi-indication commercial juggernaut, generating sales of 5.2 billion euros ($6 billion) for Sanofi in the second quarter. But the more recently launched Nemluvio is starting to carve out a place in two indications treated by Sanofi’s drug. 

Sales of Nemluvio, which the FDA approved in 2024, grew (PDF) more than 100% to $433 million in the first half of 2026. The U.S. accounted for most sales, and eczema was a bigger contributor than PN. In the U.S. from mid-June to early July, Nemluvio accounted for 42% of new patient starts in PN and 9% in eczema, Galderma said.

data.title: Pharma Doesn't Need Another Walled Garden
data.description:
In any stack, the operating system is the most tempting place to build a wall. Daily Command is the first commercial operating system for pharma, and we built it open on purpose. Here is why, and what open actually means when the outcome at stake is a prescription.

I have watched the same pattern repeat for most of my career. A platform opens to grow. It wins the market. Then it walls the market off. You can rent the audiences but never know them. Your data goes in and does not come out. Your results are graded by the same platform that sold you the media. It works beautifully, for the platform. Everyone else ends up renting access to their own customers. Pharma has paid those prices for years, and I did not want to build one more toll booth and call it infrastructure.

So when we built Daily Command, alongside the 75 senior operators who shaped it, we sat down at the exact spot where walls get built. Everything passes through the operating system. That is what makes it tempting to close. We did the opposite, on purpose. In this industry, openness is not a preference. It is an argument about outcomes.

Why pharma cannot afford walls

A pharma brand team does not start from a blank slate. They arrive with a decade of infrastructure behind them: CRM, data warehouses, clean rooms, agency systems, measurement partners, every one of them an investment somebody fought to make. Demand rip-and-replace and you punish all of it. Build open and you make it sharper instead.

And the stakes here are not the stakes everywhere else. The outcome of pharma marketing is not a click. It is a prescription, and eventually a patient on therapy. A decision that carries that much weight should never rest on a scorecard the seller controls, inside a system nobody else can see into.

What open actually means

Openness is easy to claim and easy to fake. So here is ours, in plain terms. The Doceree Marketplace, which Daily Command orchestrates through, is API-first and partner-neutral. We do not pick the winners. Brand teams do. Daily Command runs every channel and format a brand already uses, and it stays open to the analytics, data, and agency systems that brand already relies on. Intent generated inside it can be activated anywhere. Signal from anywhere flows back in. Nothing migrates, and nothing gets replaced.

Data works the same way. Teams bring their own first-party data in through secure connectors, partner integrations, or a clean room we stand up for them. If a brand has the infrastructure, we connect into it. If it needs a compliant environment, we build one. Your infrastructure or ours, the choice stays yours, because connecting activation to outcomes should never mean walking into another closed system.

Openness has to hold at the frontier too, not just across the systems a brand already owns. That is why Daily Command launched with native generative AI Connectors to OpenAI's ChatGPT and Anthropic's Claude. Healthcare's newest channel arrives open and governed from day one, carrying Semmelweis's clinical intelligence with it, instead of becoming the next place a brand gets locked in.

Open is not ungoverned

In healthcare, "open to everything" would be its own kind of failure. So the openness is governed. Any compliant platform, publisher, or partner can connect, and every connection runs on the same Clinical Intent Signals, the same identity spine, and the same compliance guardrails as every channel before it, governed by Semmelweis, which can only recommend actions that already sit within medical, legal, and regulatory guidelines. MLR, HIPAA, and GDPR are built into the substrate, not bolted on. That is not a limit on the openness. It is what makes the openness real.

Walls compound for the platform. Openness compounds for everyone.

A wall grows the platform. A network grows everyone on it. Every new connection to Daily Command makes the system sharper for every brand running on it, because every connection adds signal, and Semmelweis, our pharma-specific reasoning and orchestration model, improves with every outcome it sees. Closed systems hoard signal and call it an advantage. In healthcare, the advantage is the opposite. It is signal, connected, and governed properly.

An operating system earns the name by what it makes possible above it, not by what it traps inside it. We built Daily Command to be the opposite of a walled garden because in this industry a wall does not just cost money. It ends up standing between a brand and its outcome. It stands between a physician and the information that helps. Pharma has enough walls. What it needed was an operating system.

Daily Command is available now to pharma manufacturers, agencies, and publishers across the United States, at doceree.com/daily-command.

About Doceree

Doceree is the only healthcare marketing platform that can measure and adapt to the actual clinical intent of both physicians and patients. Built on the industry's largest real-time clinical signal network, Doceree's infrastructure unifies the entire healthcare journey — from physician awareness to prescription and patient fill to refill. Learn more at doceree.com.

data.title: Alcon survey spots gaps in teen eye care
data.description:
With back-to-school season around the corner, it’s time to load up on school supplies, fall sports gear and, as Alcon urges, eye exams. 

A recent survey from Alcon, conducted by Wakefield Research and dubbed the Alcon Student Vision Survey, interviewed 1,000 U.S. parents of teens and young adults between the ages of 13 and 25 to gauge the eye care needs of the younger generation and ran alongside Alcon’s back-to-school campaign aimed at eye care professionals. 

The survey findings show that while the majority (88%) of parents believe that their child’s vision could impact areas of school life including academic performance, class participation and confidence in the classroom, many (27%) haven’t had their teen’s vision evaluated through a comprehensive eye exam within the last year, or ever at all in some cases. 

While school eyecare screenings do help spot potential vision concerns, Alcon emphasizes that the school-based screening is only one step in supporting eye health. Among parents who delayed scheduling an eye exam for their child, 16% reported that they skipped the comprehensive exam because their teen had already passed a school screening. However, as Alcon points out, a full eye exam can help flag broader or more complex vision needs that may be overlooked during a typical screening. 

Related

Alcon gains first FDA prescription drug nod since Novartis split, scoring with drops for dry eye disease

Diving deeper into the findings, more than half (53%) of parents report that they have noticed emotional or behavioral impacts such as frustration, stress and low confidence in children who have difficulty seeing clearly, while some (21%) worry that their child may not recognize potential vision problems on their own. 

Within the parents surveyed, 42% of their children wear glasses while 23% wear contact lenses. However, 70% of parents indicated that contacts may benefit their child through convenience, sports performance and improved confidence. 

The survey confirmed that eye care professionals are considered one of the strongest drivers of action in this vein, with 45% of parents noting that a doctor’s recommendation would be their top motivator for scheduling an eye exam. To help eye doctors better reach their Gen Z patients, Alcon rolled out its Precision back-to-school campaign, offering eye care professionals a hub of resources for how to connect with their young patients and data supporting Alcon’s line of Precision contact lenses as a suitable option for the age group. 

On its campaign website, Alcon suggests that doctors ask Gen Z patients about their screen time and activities to determine if once-daily or one-week Precision lenses may be a good option. The company also supports back-to-school eye doc visits as “quick contact lens opportunities,” especially given the 31% increase in contact lens exams for patients under 25 during the summer months, Alcon notes on the site. 

Alcon picked up $4.6 billion from its vision care segment last year, with $2.8 billion attributed to its contact lens business specifically. Earlier this summer, the company rolled out a digital-first campaign to drive up awareness of LASIK eye surgery in Gen Z and Millennial audiences as an option to reduce dependence on glasses and corrective eyewear.

data.title: Amid struggles of Lilly's Foundayo, injectables still on a roll
data.description:
Eli Lilly reported $98 million in second-quarter sales for Foundayo, its newly launched oral GLP-1 treatment, lagging far behind rival Novo Nordisk's Wegovy pill. 

On Tuesday, Novo reported its quarterly results which showed that Wegovy pill generated sales of 3.22 billion Danish kroner ($497 million). In May, Novo revealed first-quarter sales of the weight-loss pill at 2.26 billion Danish kroner ($354 million) following its launch on Jan. 5, three months before Lilly received FDA approval for Foundayo on April 1.

The sales results track with IQVIA prescription data, showing that Novo’s launch has accelerated at a much quicker pace, with its first-to-market advantage playing a role.

While Foundayo’s overall result “disappointed,” according to Leerink Partners analyst David Risinger, he noted that the drug's sales in the United Arab Emirates were at $31 million, which “bodes well for Foundayo’s global potential.”

The good news for Lilly on Wednesday was that it continues to put distance between itself and Novo in revenue from its injected diabetes and obesity medicines. The Indianapolis company reported worldwide sales of Mounjaro at $9.9 billion for the second quarter, which were up 91%, and Zepbound at $4.9 billion, for a 46% year-over-year increase. 

Helping explain the disparity in sales between Lilly’s two tirzepatide products is that outside the U.S., Mounjaro is the brand name for its use in both Type 2 diabetes and obesity. 

Meanwhile, Novo reported worldwide sales of Ozempic at about 31.4 trillion Danish kroner ($4.8 billion), reflecting a 3% year-over-year increase, and of injected Wegovy at 19.5 trillion Danish kroner ($3.0 billion) for a 1% increase.

Among injectable incretins, Lilly’s drugs are now drawing three out of four new patient starts, the company said. 

Sales of Mounjaro and Zepbound fueled Lilly’s revenue for the quarter to $23 billion, which was up 48% year over year and routed analysts' consensus of $20.6 billion. The revenue figure also was a 16% sequential increase after Lilly had just a 3% sequential boost in the first quarter.

Related

The Oral GLP-1 Tracker: Foundayo, Wegovy pill reach new heights

With the result, Lilly increased the midpoint of its 2026 revenue projection from $83.5 billion to $86 billion. Its new guidance window is $85 billion to $87 billion. If the midpoint of the projection is achieved, it would provide a 32% increase from Lilly’s $65.2 billion revenue of 2025.  

Risinger said that the new projection “appears conservative,” noting that it implies flat sales in the second half.

“A caveat is that there were one-time sales benefits in the first half such as Jardiance milestone payments and onetime adjustments that benefited certain products such as Trulicity,” Risinger added.

data.title: Novo CEO stands firm on guidance amid Wegovy pill sales onslaught
data.description:
Novo’s Wegovy pill thesis continues to bear out in 2026, as the oral obesity med keeps impressive sales apace while sparing pre-existing prescriptions tied to the company’s injectable GLP-1. 

But as launches begin to take flight beyond the U.S. and the appetite for oral Wegovy builds, Novo’s manufacturing and supply chain considerations will again become a key factor in the pill’s ultimate success, analysts at Citi wrote in a note to clients Wednesday. 

In the year’s second quarter, Novo reported (PDF) net sales of 78.48 billion Danish kroner (around $12.1 billion), representing 3% growth at constant currencies. The top-line number was hampered slightly by a rebate provision reversal tied to the 340B drug pricing program last year, the company said.

Adjusted sales, on the other hand, climbed 7%, which Novo attributed in large part to GLP-1 volume growth across international markets.

Related

Novo escalates Lilly false advertising suit with planned bid to halt comparative ads

Taking a closer look at the numbers, Novo’s total obesity care sales leapt 16% at constant currencies to 23.15 billion kroner (nearly $3.6 billion). Some 19.5 billion kroner was linked to injectable Wegovy—good for a 1% increase—while around 3.22 billion kroner (nearly $500 million) originated from sales of Novo’s new obesity pill. 

Since launching the Wegovy pill at the top of the year, Novo and analysts alike have made frequent proclamations about the oral obesity med’s swift uptake, especially in light of the fact that Novo has been able to maintain an apparently substantial lead over Lilly’s rival obesity pill Foundayo, which hit the U.S. market in April.

Novo’s pill has now reached more than 5 million patients since its launch, with total weekly prescriptions for the week ending July 17 exceeding 265,000, Novo said Wednesday. Elsewhere, the pill’s launch is already transmitting positive signals in the United Arab Emirates and the United Kingdom, too, where Novo rolled out its product in June and July, respectively.

So far, Novo is “highly satisfied” with the pill’s uptake in those three markets, CFO Karsten Munk Knudsen told reporters on a media call earlier Wednesday. 

“It's important to note that the pill is mainly launched into the self-pay segment,” he explained. “So far, that’s where we’ve seen the penetration, with more than 90% of scripts coming from self-pay.” 

When the Wegovy pill launched earlier this year, Novo set a price of $149 per month for its 1.5-mg starting dose among patients paying out of pocket, with the price ticking up to $299 per month at the highest dose. 

“This is consumers paying out of pocket, and that's why we need to find the right price point that unlocks the market yet still reflects the clinical benefits of the product,” Knudsen said. 

While Novo has homed in on a Wegovy pill pricing “sweet spot” for the time being, the company will “probably” need to adjust in the future based on both the competition and consumer behavior, the CFO explained. 

The trajectory of the Wegovy pill “with limited cannibalization of injectable Wegovy” seems to confirm that the launch of an oral obesity med can meaningfully expand the market for chronic weight management, the Citi team wrote Wednesday. Meanwhile, the recent inclusion of GLP-1s on the Medicare bridge program appears to “reinforce the volume opportunity from broader access,” the analysts said. 

Nevertheless, Novo will have to make sure it can keep up with demand for its pill as it expands beyond the U.S., the Citi team cautioned, describing the “path to uninterrupted global Wegovy pill supply” as “not clearly defined.” 

“With launches broadening beyond the US and demand building rapidly, manufacturing readiness will be important to sustaining momentum without constraining access or creating uneven market availability,” the Citi team wrote, in a warning reminiscent of the shortage pitfalls both Novo and Lilly faced early in the rollouts of their injectable GLP-1s for obesity. 

To that point, Novo CEO Mike Doustdar espoused confidence in Novo’s supply chain during the company’s media call. He alluded to upcoming, targeted launches of the pill in Europe, beginning in Germany, noting that “we are making sure that we are going all in and are able to provide these medications to whoever that needs them.” 

Novo has been upfront about expectations for a tough 2026 as its attempts to redirect its business. Nevertheless, booming GLP-1 sales in the U.S. and burgeoning international launches have motivated the company to lift its full-year sales guidance, which now forecasts a 0% to 6% decline at constant currencies versus expectations for a 4% to 12% decline as of early May. 

Novo’s stock price was trading up around 3% as off 11 a.m. ET on Wednesday morning. However, the company’s share price took a tumble the day before when Novo teased its guidance update early. 

Related

Novo gains head start on Lilly with European Commission approval of Wegovy pill

Reflecting on the market reaction, Doustdar told reporters that “we don’t manage the company for today’s share price,” but rather “to create long-term value.” 

“Today’s result shows that our business is performing better than expectation, which is why we raised the guidance,” the CEO explained. 

“I have no doubt that over time the fundamentals will be reflected in the shareholder value as well,” he added.

data.title: Women turn to Reddit for community, health information: survey
data.description:
With the help of emerging internet communities on social media spaces such as Reddit, women are discovering new ways to navigate a historical gap in women’s health research, a new report finds. 

Weber Shandwick and Reddit partnered up in a July report (PDF) that aims to decode the “new health ecosystem” and the modern women’s health content discovery journey, which, as it turns out, takes place on Reddit. The partners surveyed 886 adult women and their partners in the U.S., analyzing their information-seeking behaviors across Reddit and the broader social media landscape. 

The survey findings suggest a growing preference for Reddit as a place to partake in unfiltered, anonymous discussion about health topics, with 81% of women reporting that they’re more comfortable discussing their bodies on Reddit than with their own family and friends when it comes to sensitive health topics. 

Additionally, people are turning to Reddit more and more to understand their partners’ symptoms and challenges, with 57% seeking how to offer the most helpful support to their partner during a health issue. 

The report attributes these proactive information-seeking patterns to a “profound experimental gap” between clinical guidance and lived experience, pointing to a review of National Institutes of Health (NIH) priority projects that found only 11% of priority projects from 2018 to 2020 focused on female-specific conditions. Polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS, previously known as PCOS), a common condition with hundreds of thousands of followers on a community page on Reddit, was left off of the NIH’s tracking system until 2022, the report notes. 

Related

Hologic finds women’s health stagnating over five years of global surveys

This lack of investment and focus on women’s health needs lead women to create their own communities and support systems on platforms such as Reddit, which itself is experiencing high growth across Google searches and within AI-driven searches. 

“There’s a sense of community that exists from people trying to help each other,” Weber Shandwick’s EVP of client experience, Kathleen Hunter, explained in a recent interview. 

The report marks Weber Shandwick’s second year partnering with Reddit to research women’s health topics, which has been something of a “joint passion project,” Hunter said. This year, the duo looked specifically to explore the “fragmented content discovery space” women are navigating, as the “discovery journey” evolves and grows to involve large language models and other platforms.

The findings show that these information-seeking trends also manifest in growth across women-specific subreddits, such as r/askwomenover60 with 1924% year-on-year growth, r/osteoporosis with 256% growth and r/menopause with 53% growth compared to last year, according to the report, with female Reddit users engaging with the platform across age groups and life stages, such as menopause, postpartum and more. 

“Reddit is a place that does transcend,” Hunter said, citing the “intergenerational knowledge sharing” that hallmarks the platform. 

The knowledge-sharing and community-forming nature of Reddit may also be shaped by the anonymized structure of the platform, which could foster “open, transparent conversation” in a safe environment, Fahti Khosrowshahi, founder and CEO of Ceek Women’s Health added in the interview. Ceek focuses on redesigning gynecological care and markets Nella, a modern vaginal speculum.  

“Hearing that unfiltered dialog has been really valuable,” Khosrowshahi pointed out, referring to Reddit conversations surrounding unmet needs for pelvic exams. “This is a venue where women feel safe to share their experiences, and I think specifically on sensitive topics like pelvic health and sexual trauma.” 

Although Reddit’s users are anonymous, the unbiased validation and advice from other women create a “very credible online community,” Khosrowshahi explained, noting that women will often turn to online channels to share their anxieties or concerns before bringing it up with a clinician. 

After using Reddit, 7 in 10 women reported feeling more prepared for healthcare conversations, the report found, with 47% achieving a better understanding of what is “normal versus concerning” in terms of their health, compared to 20% of non-Redditors. About 39% of those surveyed reported feeling more confident going into a doctor’s appointment over the 16% of non-Redditors who said the same. 

While Reddit can't serve as a replacement for a doctor, it can help with “bridging the gap throughout the journey,” Hunter added. 

“It’s like peeling the layers of an onion,” Khosrowshahi said. For example, in the case of understanding younger women’s anxieties over an initial pelvic exam, Reddit “allows us to slowly peel the layers of the onion to understand what is the source of the anxiety,” she explained.
